summary: AstroVital is an offline-first health-monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration missions, where communication delays of up to 22 minutes mean crews must detect and respond to health problems on their own. Each day, a crewmember completes a two-minute check-in covering vital signs, sleep, symptoms, mood and cognition, and cabin environment (CO2, radiation, temperature). A transparent, rule-based assessment engine compares every value with the astronaut's personal pre-flight baseline and with limits informed by NASA crew-health standards, and it analyzes 7-day trends such as a rising resting heart rate, accumulated sleep debt, a gradual mood decline and cumulative radiation dose. The app turns this into a colour-coded health score (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red), plain-English explanations of why each finding matters, recommended actions, and the single most useful next measurement. When the status reaches Orange or Red, it generates a Flight Surgeon Packet that is ready to send or print. AstroVital directly answers the challenge by gathering health indicators and helping astronauts evaluate and act on their own health status, supporting the Earth-independent crew autonomy that Moon and Mars missions will need.
details:
AstroVital is a complete, working web app that helps astronauts monitor and act on their own health during long missions. Live app: https://malalikhan.github.io/astrovital/

WHAT IT DOES

- Dashboard: mission day and location, an overall health score gauge (0-100), latest readings compared with the astronaut's baseline, and four colour-coded status cards: Vitals, Sleep & Recovery, Radiation & Environment, and Mood & Cognition.

- Daily Check-in: a six-step form (vitals, sleep, symptoms, mood and cognition, cabin environment, review) with a live preview of the status before saving.

- Health Trends: 7, 14 and 30-day charts for 15 metrics with baseline lines and automatically written insights.

- Assessment & Guidance: every finding explains "why this matters", gives recommended actions and the next best measurement to take.

- Flight Surgeon Packet: generated automatically at Orange or Red status, with findings, vitals vs baseline, trends and actions, ready to copy, download, print or send.

- Astronaut Passport & Settings: editable pre-flight baseline and medical summary; four mission scenarios (ISS, Lunar Gateway, Mars Transit, Mars Surface); dark/light mode; data export and import.

HOW IT WORKS

A transparent, rule-based engine checks each value against the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline (e.g. resting heart rate 20% above baseline = Orange) and fixed limits (e.g. SpO2 below 90% = Red). Trend rules look across 7 days to catch slow problems: rising heart rate, sleep debt, mood decline and cumulative radiation dose. The engine is mission-aware: expected radiation changes with the scenario, and on Mars missions critical findings tell the crew to start onboard protocols because ground support is minutes away.

HOW NASA DATA WAS USED

- NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 (Crew Health): the 600 mSv career radiation limit and the 250 mSv solar particle event limit drive the radiation budget and alerts.

- Curiosity rover RAD measurements: dose rates during the cruise to Mars (~0.48 mGy/day) and on the Martian surface (~0.21 mGy/day) set the expected daily dose for each scenario.

- NASA Human Research Program's five hazards of spaceflight (Radiation, Isolation, Distance, Gravity, Hostile environments) define the four monitoring areas.

- NASA research on sleep loss, cabin CO2, vision changes (SANS) and body-mass loss in flight shaped the thresholds and guidance.

IMPACT

Crews can catch problems days earlier, flight surgeons receive a clean structured report, and the app works fully offline, which suits Moon and Mars missions with communication delays. The same approach could help Antarctic stations, remote clinics and isolated workers.

TOOLS

HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js, Lucide icons, browser localStorage, GitHub Pages. Everything runs from one offline index.html file.

USE OF AI

The application code, documentation and slides were created with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic), directed, tested and reviewed by me. The app itself uses no AI; its assessment is rule-based. No AI-generated images are used; all images are screenshots of the working app. Sample astronaut "Cmdr. Elena Voss" is fictional; this is a prototype, not a medical device.
